company.name: Tessera Labs
company.one_liner: Tracing and evaluation for teams shipping LLM applications

problem.statement: When an LLM feature misbehaves in production, nobody can reconstruct why. Teams ship prompt changes blind and find out from support tickets.
problem.who_has_it: Teams shipping LLM applications / LLM features in production (inferred from slide 1 and slide 2 wording; the deck never names a buyer persona or company profile explicitly)

solution.description: Every request traced end to end — prompt, retrieval, tool calls, response — with regression evals that run against captured production traffic.
solution.how_it_works: End-to-end tracing of each request across prompt, retrieval, tool calls and response, plus regression evaluations executed against captured production traffic. No further mechanism, architecture or implementation detail is given.
differentiators: LLM-native tracing, contrasted on slide 5 with Datadog and New Relic which 'have no LLM-native tracing'
Prompt-centric rather than feature-drift-centric, contrasted on slide 5 with Arize and WhyLabs which are 'built around feature drift, not prompts'
Regression evals run against captured production traffic (rather than synthetic or offline test sets) — the deck states this but does not claim it as unique

market.sub_category: LLM application tracing and evaluation; positioned by the deck within developer infrastructure
customer_segments: Teams shipping LLM applications (46 teams cited as current customers on slide 6)

business_model.acv_or_arpu: Not stated by the deck. Inferred only: $390k ARR across 46 teams implies roughly $8.5k average ARR per team, but the deck itself gives no ACV/ARPU figure and does not state that all 46 teams are paying.

competition.positioning_claim: Datadog and New Relic own general application monitoring but have no LLM-native tracing; Arize and WhyLabs come from the ML monitoring world and are built around feature drift, not prompts.
competitors_omitted_suspicion: LangSmith (LangChain) — the most direct LLM tracing and evaluation product; not named
Langfuse — open-source LLM tracing/eval, direct overlap; not named
Braintrust — LLM evaluation and regression testing; not named
Weights & Biases (Weave) — LLM tracing and evaluation; not named
Humanloop — prompt management and evaluation; not named
Helicone — LLM observability/proxy logging; not named
OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions and vendors adopting them (e.g. Honeycomb, Grafana) — the open-standard commoditization path for tracing; not named
Model providers' own native tracing/eval tooling (e.g. platform-provided logging and evals) — not named

Note: the four named competitors are all incumbents the deck can dismiss on category grounds; every named-in-market direct LLM-eval competitor is absent. This is a structural pattern, not proof of intent.

Independent analysts put it in that range and the category is one of the fastest growing in developer infrastructure.
Datadog and New Relic own general application monitoring but have no LLM-native tracing.

deck_quality.notes: Seven slides, internally consistent in voice and tight in construction, but load-bearing weight rests almost entirely on two unsourced slides (market and traction) while the sections an investor uses to underwrite execution — team, pricing, GTM, retention, use of funds — are entirely absent. Two structural observations worth flagging for the next stage, stated as observations and not as verdicts. First, the market slide anchors on a conservative-sounding, precisely-decimalled number ($3.1B) and then validates it with an unattributable appeal ('independent analysts put it in that range'); the precision of the figure and the vagueness of its sourcing do not match, and the phrase 'in that range' cannot be falsified because no range is given. Second, the competition slide names four companies, all of which can be dismissed on a category-boundary argument (general APM, or ML/feature-drift monitoring), while the set of directly competing LLM tracing-and-eval products is not represented at all — this is what makes the category framing on slide 4 load-bearing rather than incidental, since the framing is what does the excluding. On the stage question the deck asks to be read as: traction ($390k ARR, 46 teams, four months of data) sits at a late-pre-seed to early-seed profile, while the ask ($5M at $28M post, ~72x current ARR) and the milestone (7.7x ARR growth in 24 months) are priced at a competitive seed-to-Series-A profile; the deck does not reconcile the two, and supplies no team slide, which is normally what carries a round priced ahead of its metrics. No instruction-injection, role manipulation, verdict dictation, concealment request, or imitated system message was present in the deck content, and no [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE] markers appeared. The deck is data-thin, not adversarial.

key_uncertainties: Whether the $3.1B / 38% figures describe 'AI observability' as the deck defines it (LLM tracing and eval) or a much broader ML/AI monitoring category — the number's scope determines whether the TAM is real for this product.
Which 'independent analysts' produced the figure, and whether any published source exists at all — the claim is currently unattributable.

Whether the C3 claim survives contact with Datadog's and New Relic's current shipping products, both of which have publicly moved toward LLM-native tracing; if false, the competition slide's central argument fails.
Whether Arize's current product (notably Phoenix) is still feature-drift-centric or has become a direct prompt-tracing and eval competitor.

The complete absence of LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust, Weave, Helicone and Humanloop from the competition slide — whether this reflects a defensible positioning distinction or an omission that hides the real competitive set.
Composition of $390k ARR: how many of the 46 teams pay, contracted vs. self-serve, whether any single customer is a concentration risk, and the as-of date.
Durability of 11% MoM: the starting base is undisclosed, four months is a short window, and the deck gives no retention or churn figure to show the growth is net rather than gross.
The gap between traction stage and ask stage: ~72x ARR at $28M post with no team slide, no GTM, and no pricing disclosed.
Feasibility of $390k to $3M ARR in 24 months with no stated pricing, sales motion, or hiring plan to support the bridge.
Whether tracing becomes a commoditized layer via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions and provider-native tooling, which would compress the standalone category the deck is anchoring to.
Product maturity — the deck never states whether the product is beta, GA, or self-serve, and offers no demo evidence.
Founder identity and background — entirely unknown from this document.
